newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions say Elf turned down deal on strike talks.
newsitem.headline: Unions say Elf turned down deal on strike talks.

text.p: Striking Elf Aquitaine refinery workers have failed to get their full demands including early retirement on the agenda in advance of talks set for later on Tuesday, union officials said.
One senior union official said Elf had refused an offer to unblock deliveries from three stricken French refineries in return for a pledge to negotiate on all the strikers' demands.
An Elf spokesman did not comment on whether an offer of a deal had been turned down, but confirmed there was no agenda for talks between union delegates and managers slated for 1400 GMT.
"There is a meeting scheduled. That is all," he said.
"There is no real plan on what to discuss. They don't have an agenda," he said.

The strike crippling a quarter of French refinery production at three Elf plants, now in its sixth day, began as a one-day protest over job cuts last week but now embraces a list of union demands including more pay and pensions at 55 for shift workers.
The union official said he was disappointed about the lack of an agenda for Tuesday's talks, the first since the strike began in separate stages last Wednesday and Thursday.
He predicted the strike would continue.

"We proposed to open the valves to let some lorries out on condition the management agreed to open negotiations," he said. "Elf refused and has simply agreed to meet the national (union) delegates," he said.
"Therefore both production and deliveries remain stopped and I think the dispute will go on," he added.
Other union officials were less pessimistic, saying Elf managers had tried to cooperate at local level but their efforts were being blocked at Elf's Paris headquarters.
Elf has said the strike is not causing fuel shortages since tanks at supply depots outside the refineries are full in the wake of a 12-day truckers' blockade which ended on Friday.
It says its plans to cut 10 percent of staff at refining subsidiary Elf Antar are necessary to allow it to compete and it accuses unions of raising their demands since the strike began.
